result.document_summary: Part 1 of 4 of the NJ Department of Community Affairs 'Truth in Renting' guide, summarizing NJ landlord-tenant law including lease renewal/just-cause non-renewal and the start of the Security Deposit Law.
result.notes: Part 1 covers the lease, termination, right of entry and the beginning of security deposits. Rent control, eviction causes, and credit/background checks fall in later parts and are not extracted here. The security deposit return deadlines and interest rules continue in the next part; only the cap and exemption stated here are captured. The non-renewal good-cause statement is a brief cross-reference; detailed causes appear later in the guide.

rules.title: Security deposit cap of 1.5 months' rent
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rents held as security (including last month's rent) count toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
rules.key_value: 1.5x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
rules.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ). It can be less.
rules.coverage_text: Most residential rental properties in New Jersey, including mobile homes, except owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings (unless the tenant elects coverage by written request).
rules.exemptions_text: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt, though the tenant may make the law apply 30 days after sending a written request to the landlord.
rules.interaction: The first month's rent may be collected in addition, so no more than 2.5 times monthly rent in total at lease inception. The interest-bearing account provisions do not apply to seasonal rentals.

rules.title: Good cause required for lease non-renewal (Anti-Eviction Act)
rules.requirement: Landlords of residential rental properties may not fail to renew a written or oral lease unless they have a statutory good cause, and a landlord may terminate a lease only by offering new terms the tenant rejects; the lease ending alone is not a basis for eviction. The listed good causes are detailed in the guide's Eviction section.
